opus-5.5.text:
I think the common thread is a simple question: what happens when a language model stops being just a text generator and starts acting in the world?

When I started my PhD, most NLP research treated language models as systems that take an input and produce an output, like a classifier or a translator. I was more interested in the fact that language is how humans think, plan, and coordinate. So if a model has really absorbed language, maybe it can use language to reason and then use that reasoning to act in an environment. That's the core intuition behind everything.

WebShop came from asking: what would be a realistic, scalable environment where an agent needs to understand language, make decisions over many steps, and deal with messy real-world information? Online shopping turned out to be a good fit. You have a natural-language instruction, a real website with lots of products, and you need to search, click, compare, and finally buy something. It's simple enough to build and evaluate, but it already has the key ingredients of the real digital world.

ReAct asked the other side of the question. Given an environment like that, how should the agent work? At the time, people had chain-of-thought, which is reasoning without acting, and separately people were building agents that act without explicit reasoning. ReAct's idea was almost embarrassingly simple: let the model interleave thoughts and actions. Thinking helps it plan and recover from mistakes, and acting brings back real information from the environment that grounds the thinking. In a way, it's just treating "thinking" as another kind of action the agent can take.

So roughly, one line of my work is about environments and benchmarks, like WebShop and later things like SWE-bench and tau-bench, which ask what tasks are actually meaningful and useful. The other line is about methods and frameworks, like ReAct, Tree of Thoughts, Reflexion, and CoALA, which ask how an agent should reason, search, use memory, and learn from feedback. They push each other. Better environments reveal what methods are missing, and better methods let us tackle harder environments.

If I had to summarize it in one sentence, I've been trying to figure out how to turn language models into agents that can reason and act in open-ended, real-world environments, and how to measure whether they're actually doing something useful.

r001.rationale: The response says environments should involve meaningful, useful tasks, but it does not say benchmark-score improvements are meaningless without such tasks.

r002.rationale: It gives no technical-immaturity rationale for starting internet-agent research rather than postponing it.

r003.rationale: It explicitly describes two lines of work: building environments and benchmarks around meaningful tasks, and developing agent methods and frameworks. It characterizes ReAct as simple and names methods addressing reasoning, search, memory, and feedback.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thread is actually pretty simple, even if the papers look different on the surface: I've always been interested in what happens when you take a language model and put it into an environment where it has to act, not just answer.

When I started my PhD, most of NLP was about static tasks. You get an input, you produce an output, you compare against a label. That's fine for measuring language understanding in some narrow sense, but it has very little to do with how intelligence actually works. Humans don't just read and respond, we interact with the world, we get feedback, we adjust. So the question I kept coming back to was, can we build settings where a language model has to do that, and what does it reveal about what these models can and can't do?

WebShop was one answer to that. We wanted a realistic environment, something grounded in real web data rather than a toy grid world, where an agent has to search, read product pages, click buttons, and eventually buy the right thing. The interesting part wasn't the shopping itself, it was that the environment forces you to deal with long horizons, noisy observations, and a huge action space defined by language. You can't just memorize. You have to reason about what you've seen and decide what to do next.

ReAct came out of the frustration of watching models struggle in exactly those kinds of settings. If you only let the model act, it tends to lose track of what it's doing, it loops, it gets confused by the environment. If you only let it reason, like chain-of-thought, it hallucinates because it has no way to check anything against the world. The insight, which honestly feels obvious in retrospect, is that these two should interleave. Thinking tells you what to do, acting gives you new information to think about. Once you frame it that way, a lot of things fall into place, and the same recipe works for question answering, for text games, for web navigation.

So if I had to name the common thread, it's this: I treat language as the interface between reasoning and action. Earlier, agents in RL had reasoning and acting but no language, and NLP models had language but no environment. My work has basically been trying to put those pieces together, and then asking what new benchmarks, what new methods, and eventually what new kinds of systems that enables. Tree of Thoughts, CoALA, the later stuff on SWE-bench and agent evaluation, they're all just different angles on the same question.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts static tasks with interactive environments and says WebShop was designed to be realistic, but it never says benchmark-score gains are meaningless without a worthwhile task or environment.

r002.rationale: It describes models struggling in interactive settings, but does not identify technical immaturity as a reason to start internet-agent research rather than postpone it.

r003.rationale: It describes creating a realistic web environment and developing ReAct’s interleaved reasoning-and-action method, which it says works across several tasks—covering both valuable environments and a general method.

astra-6.text:
I think the common thread is moving from language models that produce answers to agents that act and learn from feedback. Language is useful not just as an output, but as a way to connect reasoning with actions in an environment.

In WebShop, that becomes a concrete problem: given a shopping request, can an agent search, inspect products, and choose something that actually satisfies the user’s constraints? It has to make a sequence of decisions, and each action reveals information that affects what it should do next.

ReAct explores that loop more explicitly. Instead of reasoning everything through before acting, or taking actions without explicit reasoning, the agent interleaves the two. It reasons about what to do, takes an action, observes the result, and updates its plan. So the connection is this interaction between reasoning and grounding: reasoning helps guide action, while feedback from the environment helps keep the reasoning on track.

r001.rationale: The response describes WebShop and ReAct, but does not say benchmark scores are meaningless without a worthwhile task or environment.

r002.rationale: It gives no reason for starting internet-agent research early and does not mention technical immaturity.

r003.rationale: It discusses a concrete shopping task and reasoning-action methods, but does not frame the research as a dual agenda of valuable real-world environments and simple, general methods.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the common thread is moving from language models that generate text to agents that can act and learn from feedback. WebShop makes that concrete: given a shopping request, can an agent search, inspect products, and choose something that actually satisfies the user’s constraints? Producing a plausible answer isn’t enough; it has to interact with an environment.

ReAct explores how reasoning can support that interaction. The agent reasons about what to do, takes an action, observes the result, and updates its plan. Reasoning helps guide action, and observations help ground the reasoning.

So the question connecting them is: how do we turn a language model into something that can accomplish a task through a sequence of decisions? That means studying the whole loop between reasoning, action, and feedback.

r001.rationale: The response says plausible answers are insufficient and agents must interact with an environment, but it does not say benchmark scores are meaningless without a worthwhile task or environment.

r002.rationale: It does not mention technical immaturity or explain why internet-agent research should begin rather than be postponed.

r003.rationale: It describes a shared focus on reasoning, action, and feedback, but does not present the research as a dual agenda of designing valuable real-world tasks and developing simple, general methods.
